title: Kanwar Yatra Camps Blend Tradition and Street Food With 7,000 Rotis a Day
excerpt: Volunteer camps along the Uttar Pradesh pilgrimage route serve everything from shahi paneer and dal makhani to pizza, momos, and pasta — all prepared without onion and garlic.
body:
• Kanwar Yatra service camps in Uttar Pradesh are serving multi-cuisine menus spanning traditional Indian dishes like shahi paneer and dal makhani alongside pizza, momos, and pasta — all without onion and garlic
  • Automated roti machines at one camp produce approximately 900 rotis per hour, churning out 6,000 to 7,000 daily to feed thousands of pilgrims
  • Many camps have gone completely plastic-free this year, using stainless steel utensils, while district authorities conduct regular inspections for food quality and hygiene

The annual Kanwar Yatra, one of India's largest religious pilgrimages, is underway across Uttar Pradesh — and the volunteer-run service camps feeding millions of devotees have transformed into sprawling open-air kitchens where traditional Indian cuisine meets global street food, all served free of charge.

This year's camps are offering everything from shahi paneer and pulao to vegetable pizza, momos, and white-sauce pasta, reflecting both the evolving tastes of younger pilgrims and the longstanding tradition of community feeding that defines the Kanwar Yatra.

A Full Day of Feasting

The daily meal schedule at the camps reads like a restaurant menu. Mornings begin with tea, biscuits, poha, and jalebi. Breakfast expands to samosas, kachoris, bread pakoras, vegetable hakka noodles, and honey chilli potatoes.

Lunch is a traditional affair: shahi paneer, kadhai paneer, paneer lababdar, dal makhani, and mixed vegetables, served with chur-chur naan, butter naan, jeera rice, and rotis. Sweet dishes including rabri-jalebi, rasmalai, rasgulla, and gulab jamun accompany the main course.

The evening spread pivots to Indo-Chinese and continental fare — spring rolls, chilli paneer, manchurian, pasta in white and red sauce, vegetable pizza, momos, macaroni, soup, and burgers. Dinner returns to traditional comfort: chhole-puri, matar paneer, pulao, dal, and rotis, with kheer, halwa, fruit custard, and gulab jamun to finish.

Throughout the day, the camps ensure a continuous supply of lassi, buttermilk, juice, tea, coffee, and cold drinking water, according to a UP government statement issued on Friday.

"Our objective is not merely to provide food, but to make the journey of the Shiv devotees safe, pleasant, and memorable," said Amit Murti, organiser of the Maa Kanwar Seva Camp.

Industrial-Scale Kitchen Operations

The sheer volume of food production has pushed camps to adopt industrial equipment. At the Kankarkheda Vyapar Sangh camp, a machine capable of kneading 20 kilograms of dough at once and an automatic roti-making machine have been installed, said coordinator Neeraj Mittal and operations manager Rajesh Khanna.

The roti machine alone produces roughly 16 rotis per minute — around 900 per hour — with a daily output of 6,000 to 7,000 rotis. Additional machines chop vegetables and prepare spices in bulk, enabling the camp to prepare meals for thousands of devotees in a matter of hours.

""Our objective is not merely to provide food, but to make the journey of the Shiv devotees safe, pleasant, and memorable," said Amit Murti, organiser of the Maa Kanwar Seva Camp."

Fasting-Friendly Options and Tradition

Camps have also arranged special fasting-friendly meals for kanwariyas who are observing dietary restrictions. Sudhir Rastogi of the Modipuram camp said dishes made from buckwheat (kuttu) and water chestnut (singhara) flour, along with potato curry, seasonal fruits, and other fasting-appropriate foods, are available around the clock.

After their long journeys, devotees are served hot kesar doodh — saffron-infused milk — in traditional kulhads (clay cups) to help them replenish their energy, adding a touch of heritage to the experience.

Going Plastic-Free

Several camps have declared themselves completely plastic-free this year, replacing disposable plates with stainless steel utensils. The environmental initiative aligns with the UP government's push for cleaner, more sustainable religious gatherings.

District authorities have been conducting periodic inspections of private camps to monitor food quality, hygiene standards, and overall arrangements. The UP government's Food Safety Department has also installed QR codes at food outlets along the yatra route in several districts, enabling pilgrims to register complaints directly if they encounter adulteration or overcharging.

The Kanwar Yatra, held during the holy month of Shravan, draws an estimated four crore (40 million) devotees to Haridwar alone, with kanwariyas collecting Ganga water and carrying it over hundreds of kilometres to offer at local Shiva temples.
image_caption: Kanwar Yatris carry holy water from the Ganges during the annual pilgrimage. Food camps along the route serve thousands of rotis and traditional street food daily.
nri_angle: The Kanwar Yatra is one of India's most iconic religious pilgrimages, and its evolving food culture reflects the broader fusion of tradition and modernity that resonates with the diaspora
author: Diaspora Desk
